newsitem.title: USA: With one brokerage mega-deal done, who's next?.
newsitem.headline: With one brokerage mega-deal done, who's next?.

text.p: The surprise joining between Morgan Stanley Group Inc and Dean Witter, Discover & Co reshapes the financial services landscape and focuses immediate attention on who will be next to merge.

"Nothing is outside the realm of possibility," said Lawrence Rice, chief investment officer at Josephthal, Lyon & Ross. "You've got banks, insurance companies and even other brokerages all looking to make deals."
The $10.2 billion deal announced today combines investment banking and retail in a way others are likely to try to emulate, analysts said.
Several analysts had predicted a wave of consolidation would come as firms moved to fill voids in their business lines.
In recent months, speculation swirled about bids for Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc and PaineWebber Group Inc, itself formerly viewed as a possible partner for Morgan Stanley.

Today, some mused Lehman and PaineWebber could turn to each other, marrying the former's investment banking prowess to the latter's retail business. But while such a link might have surface appeal, analysts were uninspired by the prospect.

"Lehman will go to someone who's primarily interested in capital markets and PaineWebber will go to someone who's primarily interested in retail," said Perrin Long, an independent analyst who covers the securities industry.
"But both have pre-tax profit margins way below industry averages and normally if you take two weak sisters and put them together, you won't get a stronger entity," Long said.
As it happened, the industry's consolidation took a different turn, creating a Wall Street presence rivaling even Merrill Lynch and Co Inc in size and scope.

In terms of revenues, Merrill Lynch still stands well atop the field, analysts said, but in other ways, like asset management, the combined Morgan Stanley-Dean Witter eclipses Merrill Lynch as the securities industry's leader.
Morgan Stanley-Dean Witter's combined asset management unit will direct some $270 billion in assets, compared with $234 billion at Merrill Lynch Asset Management at the end of 1996.

Perhaps more importantly, other firms will now be forced to combat Morgan's combination of investment banking and retail operations and its ability to market products and services to Discover's 39 million credit card customers.
Share prices in a number of regional brokers also spiked higher in anticipation of the next step in an industry shake-up, among them Alex. Brown Inc, A.G. Edwards Inc and Legg Mason Inc.
All three were all among a group cited by Oppenheimer & Co analyst Steven Eisman as potential takeover candidates.
Eisman, whose opinion on the regionals appeared in a research note last October, confirmed today he still viewed group members as potential acquisition targets.

In contrast to others in the sector, shares in PaineWebber fell sharply today, partially reversing a recent run-up that had become so intense that the NYSE yesterday sought a comment from the company.
PaineWebber declined to offer one, citing a company policy against commenting on market activity or rumors.
A Morgan Stanley spokeswoman later flatly denied that company was in merger talks -- with PaineWebber.
